title: TB0-02396
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: XXXXXXXX (a.k.a. XXXXXXX) (the claimant) is a citizen of the People's Republic of China (China).1 He claims refugee protection pursuant to section 96 and subsection 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.

The claimant alleges that his wife had an affair and he became angry and sad and he began to drink and lose confidence in his future life. A friend visited him in XXXXXX 2008 and spread the gospel to him. He attended his first service in an underground church on XXXXXX, 2008. The church was raided on XXXXXX, 2009. He escaped and went into hiding. Subsequently he learned that the Public Security Bureau (PSB) came to his home and accused him of involvement in illegal religious activities. They left a summons with his family the next day. As a result, he left China. The PSB is still looking for him.
The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection.

The determinative issue in regard to this claim is the credibility of the claimant's oral testimony and Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative2 concerning his alleged membership in an underground church that was raided by the PSB, his pursuit by the PSB and his jeopardy if he were to return to China. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is not a credible witness in this regard. THE CLAIMANT'S MEMBERSHIP IN AN UNDERGROUND CHURCH IN CHINA

The claimant testified that when his wife had an affair, he became angry and depressed. A friend spread the gospel to him and he joined his friend's underground church. In general, he testified in this regard in a straight-forward manner, with no significant inconsistencies. In addition, the claimant provided a full description of a church service in China with and without a pastor. I have no basis to challenge his testimony and PIF narrative that he was a practicing Christian in China.

The claimant's alleged membership in an underground church is more difficult to judge. He testified that there were XX members in his underground church and they met every three weeks in a house in the suburbs, with the next door neighbour approximately 20 metres away. He further testified that he was told there had been no problems before he allegedly joined this church and he was able to attend without incident for approximately one year. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that it is reasonable to assume that if this group feared PSB notice, as reflected in the claimant's testimony regarding lookouts and other precautions, 42 people would not meet regularly in a house in the suburbs where neighbours might observe them and authorities might be informed. In addition, country documentary evidence3 indicates that a PSB raid on an underground church in his province is not likely. COUNTRY DOCUMENTARY EVIDENCE REGARDING REPRESSION OF UNDERGROUND CHURCHES IN CHINA GENERALLY AND SPECIFICALLY IN LIAONING PROVINCE

The claimant is a resident of Liaoning province. The U.S. State Department 2010 International Religious Freedom Report4 notes a range of arrests in various specifically identified provinces but makes no mention of any arrests in Liaoning province. This document further indicates that the ability of unregistered religious groups to operate varied greatly depending on the location. As noted above, there is evidence of suppression by Chinese authorities in a number of provinces but not in Liaoning province. It is also noted that most Christian groups, the majority of which are unregistered, no longer operate secretly. Instead, they carry out their activities openly. In this regard, another country document5 quotes the President of ChinaSource, an organization that assists members of international faith-based communities to work in China: "while reports of persecution remain a reality of life in China, a survey of the larger picture suggests that they are the exception rather than the rule...."

In addition, the Annual Report of Persecution by the Government on Christian Churches within Mainland China,6 published by the United States based China Aid Association, specifically notes information concerning arrests as well as evidence of persecution in various provinces. None of the incidents noted occurred in Liaoning province. Although country documentary evidence regarding China generally provides mixed messages concerning the suppression of underground church activity, the lack of any information regarding instances of arrests and other forms of persecution for Liaoning province in any of the documents available to the panel is significant and convincing. This does not mean that there is no possibility that an underground church community might be harassed by the PSB. However, there is information regarding suppression in a number of small provinces but none regarding this large province. I find, on a balance of probabilities and on the basis of documentary evidence cited above, that the claimant's alleged underground church would not be of any interest to the PSB in Liaoning province.

I am supported in the above decision by a recent decision by Mr. Justice Russell.7 While this decision concerns an alleged raid in Guangdong province and Fujian province evidence is also cited, the lack of recent evidence concerning repression of underground church members and communities in Liaoning province replicates the situation in regard to those two provinces.

In addition, in reaching his decision, Mr. Justice Russell cited Justice Crampton's decision in Lin8 concerning Fujian province in which the court stated that in the context of the significant detail in the documentation regarding the dates and locations of arrests and other steps taken to discourage Christian activity in China, it was reasonable for the Board to conclude that if persecution of members of underground churches occurred in Fujian province, it would have been documented.

As well, in Yu,9 Justice Zinn noted that the only evidence provided to the Board regarding the alleged raid was the claimant's own testimony and there was documentary evidence before the Board that brought his evidence of the raid into question and lead to an inference that no such raid occurred.

The claimant disclosed a summons document10 allegedly left with his family. However, the format and content of this document is quite different from the models and description available in country documentary evidence.11 In this regard, a summons is prepared in triplicate. The original is retained by the PSB and a copy is signed and dated by the person receiving the summons and taken by the PSB. The third copy is left with the person who received the summons. The alleged summons disclosed by the claimant is an original document. In addition, there is no signature on the claimant's disclosure acknowledging receipt of the summons. As well, documentary evidence indicates that the names of the two persons involved with the issuance and delivery of the summons are to be noted in the document. These names are not included in the claimant's disclosure. It is reasonable to assume that the inclusion of these names is important in regard to required follow-up concerning the appearance or lack of appearance of the person being summoned and any further PSB or judicial action.

The documentary evidence12 also indicates that the address and unit number of the person being summoned is to be included in the summons. However, this information is not included in the document disclosed by the claimant. By relying on common sense, in the panel's opinion, it is reasonable to assume that the PSB document would include the address of the person named in the summons since this information would be required by the serving officer to correctly identify the location of the individual's known address to effect service of the document. Counsel indicated in her submissions that this document was likely a summons for interrogation and that could account for the differences. However, similar requirements for the inclusion of an address, unit number, and the names of two issuing officials are noted in the example of a summons for interrogation and there is no indication in the descriptive section that a summons for interrogation would not be issued in triplicate with the original retained by the PSB.

While there may well be regional differences in the format of a summons, the lack of the most basic and useful elements in the document disclosed by the claimant is significant. The claimant was unable to explain the differences in this document. I note that the summons is the one document that might have corroborated the claimant's testimony regarding the raid and his pursuit by the PSB. However, I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the document disclosed by the claimant is fraudulent. Country documentary evidence indicates that such fraudulent documents are commonly manufacture and easily purchased in China.13 In this regard, the panel notes that this specific analysis concerning deficiencies in PSB summons documents has been recently considered by the federal Court in two separate instances and found not to be unreasonable.14

I further find, on a balance of probabilities and in the context of findings and negative inferences noted above, as well as the country documentary evidence and case law cited above, that while the claimant may have been a practicing Christian in China, he was not a member of an underground church in China that was raided by the PSB, and that he is not being pursued by the PSB.

The claimant was able to answer correctly a number of questions concerning Christian teachings, and the teachings of Pentecostal Christianity in particular, and his responses appeared to reflect commitment and belief. In addition, he disclosed a letter from his pastor15 confirming his church membership. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant is now a genuine practicing Christian and that he likely was a practicing Christian in China. THE ALLEGED CONSTRAINTS ON THE CLAIMANT'S ABILITY TO PRACTICE HIS RELIGION FREELY IF HE WERE TO RETURN TO CHINA

Counsel emphasized the constraint on the claimant's ability to spread the gospel in public in China, a practice that is central to Pentecostal teachings. However, country documentary evidence16 indicates that although public proselytizing is constrained by the Government in China, it is possible to do so if it is not done in a public place such as a city square or government offices. It was also noted by the Executive Secretary of the Hong Kong Christian Council that he had attended and participated in open air evangelist campaigns sanctioned by local government. It is further noted that government responses to proselytizing varies from place to place. In this regard, it is reasonable to assume that the places where proselytizing would be allowed are those, like Liaoning province, where there is no recent evidence of repression of underground church activity. I find, on a balance of probabilities, that the claimant would be able to participate in proselytizing activities and the constraints noted above do not rise to the level of persecution.

I therefore find on the basis of the totality of evidence noted above, in particular on the basis of documentary evidence and case law cited above, that the claimant can return to his home in Liaoning province and practice his religion freely. I therefore find that the claimant has failed to satisfy his onus of establishing a serious possibility that he would be persecuted or that he would be personally subjected to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment, or a risk to his life, or a risk of torture by any authority in the People's Republic of China.

The claimant is neither a Convention refugee nor a person in need of protection. Therefore, the Refugee Protection Division rejects his claim.
